title: NoSQL with Azure Cosmos DB (Basic)
reading:
Today's menu

By the end of this lunch you will be able to:

- Explain the four NoSQL data models and choose the right Azure Cosmos DB API for a workload.
- Describe how accounts, databases, containers and items fit together, and how request units are billed in provisioned, autoscale, serverless and free-tier setups.
- Choose a partition key that spreads data and traffic evenly, and spot a hot partition before it hurts.
- Compare the five consistency levels and decide when Cosmos DB, rather than Azure SQL, is the right home for your data.

Meanwhile at Nusantara Retail

Dewi drops a printout on your desk: the Products table from the storefront database. It has 140 columns, and most rows leave more than a hundred of them empty. Coffee needs a roast level and a grind, batik needs a fabric and a size chart, the new rattan baskets need dimensions. Every new product type means another schema change, another late-night migration and, usually, another bug.

Marketing wants a mobile app before the 12.12 sale, when catalogue traffic can jump twentyfold in an hour. Ibu Sari has two questions of her own: can we pay only for what shoppers actually use, and can customers in Medan and Makassar get pages as fast as customers in Jakarta?

Orders and payments can stay in Azure SQL from Lunch 11 — they need relational rules. The catalogue is a different animal. Today's question: where should a catalogue that changes shape every week, and must stay fast during a sale-day spike, live?

Reading

1. NoSQL in one page: data models and Cosmos DB APIs

A relational database stores rows in tables with a fixed schema, joins tables at query time and wraps changes in transactions that can touch many tables. That model is excellent for orders and money. It is less comfortable when every record wants a different shape, or when one server can no longer keep up.

NoSQL ("not only SQL") databases relax some of those rules to gain flexibility and scale. They usually offer a flexible schema, horizontal scale-out across many machines, and very fast reads and writes by key. In exchange you give up most joins, and transactions shrink to a smaller scope. NoSQL is not "better" than relational; it is a different set of trade-offs. There are four common data models:

Data model | Shape of the data | Nusantara Retail example | Cosmos DB API
Document | Self-describing JSON documents; each can carry its own fields | A coffee with a roast level next to a batik shirt with sizes | API for NoSQL, API for MongoDB
Key-value | A value fetched by one unique key | A shopping cart looked up by its cart ID | API for Table (and point reads in any API)
Column-family | Wide rows whose columns can differ, grouped into families | Footfall-sensor readings per store, per minute | API for Apache Cassandra
Graph | Vertices (things) joined by edges (relationships) | "Shoppers who bought kopi also bought…" | API for Apache Gremlin

Azure Cosmos DB is Azure's fully managed NoSQL database. Microsoft runs the servers, replicas, patching and backups; you get automatic indexing, replication to as many regions as you like, and a latency commitment: reads and writes under 10 ms at the 99th percentile (with an exception for strong consistency across several regions, covered in section 4).

You pick an API when you create an account, and you can't change it later. The API decides which wire protocol, drivers and query language your application uses:

- API for NoSQL — the native API: JSON items, a SQL-like query language, and new features (such as vector search) first. It is the default choice for new applications.
- API for MongoDB — speaks the MongoDB wire protocol, so existing Mongo apps and tools move across with few changes. The vCore-based MongoDB offering became a separate product in November 2025: Azure DocumentDB.
- API for Apache Cassandra and API for Apache Gremlin — for existing Cassandra (CQL) and graph applications.
- API for Table — a key-value API for apps written for Azure Table Storage that need more speed or global reach.

Azure Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL still appears in older material. It is on a retirement path and new deployments are blocked; Microsoft points distributed PostgreSQL work to elastic clusters in Azure Database for PostgreSQL instead.

Tip: Starting from scratch? Choose API for NoSQL. The other APIs exist mainly to bring existing applications across without a rewrite. Everything in this lunch and its lab uses API for NoSQL.

2. Accounts, containers and request units

Cosmos DB organises everything in four levels:

- The account is the top-level resource with a globally unique name and its own endpoint (https://<account>.documents.azure.com). Regions, the API, the default consistency level and the capacity mode are account settings.
- A database is a namespace that groups containers. It can optionally share throughput between its containers.
- A container is the unit of scale. You choose its partition key when you create it, and it holds the indexing policy and optional time to live (TTL), which deletes items automatically after a set period — perfect for abandoned carts.
- An item is one JSON document of up to 2 MB. Every item needs an id, which must be unique within its partition key value. Items in the same container don't need the same fields: the coffee and the batik shirt live side by side.

Every operation costs request units (RUs), a single currency that blends CPU, memory and I/O. Reading one 1 KB item by its id and partition key — a point read — costs 1 RU. Writes cost more, because every write also updates the indexes. A query's cost depends on how much data it has to touch. The same query over the same data always costs the same, and every response reports its charge, so you can measure instead of guess.

That makes capacity planning a spreadsheet exercise rather than a hardware guess. Suppose the storefront serves 300 product pages per second (one point read each, about 1 RU) and 100 category pages per second (one query each, say 3 RU after you measure it). That is 300 + 300 = 600 RU/s of reads. Add the writes from stock updates, round up for the sale, and you have a number to provision — or a reason to choose serverless while traffic is still small.

How you pay for RUs depends on the capacity mode you choose for the account:

Mode | You pay for | Good for | Watch out for
Provisioned, manual | The RU/s you reserve, per hour (at least 400 RU/s per container) | Steady, predictable traffic | You pay for idle capacity; requests above it are throttled with HTTP 429
Provisioned, autoscale | The highest RU/s used each hour, between 10% and 100% of a maximum you set | Spiky traffic, such as the 12.12 sale | The floor is 10% of the maximum, even when idle
Serverless | Only the RUs you consume, plus storage | Development, testing, low or bursty traffic | Single region only; costs vary with usage, so watch the meter
Free tier (a discount on provisioned) | Nothing for the first 1,000 RU/s and 25 GB, for the lifetime of the account | Learning and small production apps | One free-tier account per subscription, chosen at creation; not available for serverless

When a request needs more RU/s than the container has, Cosmos DB answers with HTTP 429 "request rate too large" and the SDK retries after a short wait. Occasional 429s are normal; constant 429s mean you need more throughput or a better design.

Warning: Provisioned throughput is billed in every region of the account: 1,000 RU/s in three regions is 3,000 RU/s on the bill. And because free tier is one account per subscription and can only be switched on at creation time, it is easy to "use it up" on a forgotten experiment. Check before you create: the portal greys the option out if it's taken.

3. Partitioning: the one decision you can't undo

Cosmos DB scales by splitting a container across many machines, and the partition key decides how. All items with the same partition key value form a logical partition: every coffee product when the key is /category. A logical partition holds up to 20 GB, and it is also the boundary for transactions — a stored procedure or transactional batch can only change items that share one partition key value.

Behind the scenes, Cosmos DB hashes each key value and places logical partitions on physical partitions, the replica sets that do the work. You never manage physical partitions; Cosmos DB splits them as data and throughput grow. What you need to know is their ceiling: one physical partition serves up to 10,000 RU/s and 50 GB, so a single logical partition can never use more than that. A hot partition is one key value that receives far more traffic than the rest. It hits the ceiling and gets throttled while the other partitions sit idle.

A good partition key has a wide range of values, spreads both storage and requests evenly, never changes for an item, and appears as an equality filter in your most frequent queries. The practical method is to start from the queries, not from the data: list the five requests your app makes most often, note which property each one filters on, and look for the property that appears in most of them. When no single property works, you can build a synthetic key by joining two values, such as JKT-01|2026-12-12. Here are Nusantara Retail's candidates:

Container | Candidate key | Verdict | Why
products | /category | Fine for a catalogue | A few thousand items, read-heavy, and most pages ask "everything in this category". Few values, so keep an eye on a "promo" category during the sale.
products | /id | Possible | Perfect spread and cheap point reads, but every category page becomes a cross-partition query.
orders | /storeId | Hot partition | Only 41 values, and the online store takes most orders; one store's history also grows toward the 20 GB limit.
orders | /orderDate | Hot partition | Every write today lands on today's value — the classic anti-pattern.
orders | /orderId | Good for writes | Spreads writes perfectly and supports point reads by order number, but "show my orders" must ask every partition.
orders | /customerId | Best fit | High cardinality and matches the "my orders" page. If a few corporate buyers grow huge, use hierarchical keys.

When a query includes the partition key, Cosmos DB sends it to one physical partition. When it doesn't, it becomes a cross-partition query that fans out to every physical partition, adding roughly 2–3 RU per partition plus extra latency. In a small container with one physical partition you barely notice; with fifty partitions, every search costs fifty times the overhead.

You can't change a container's partition key in place: you create a new container and copy the data across (container copy jobs help). If one level isn't enough, hierarchical partition keys let you combine up to three levels, such as /customerId then /orderId.

4. Going global: regions and the five consistency levels

Adding a region to a Cosmos DB account takes a single click or command. Each region holds a full copy of the data, your application reads from the nearest one, and provisioned RU/s apply in every region. By default one region accepts writes and the others serve reads; with multi-region writes, every region accepts writes and Cosmos DB resolves conflicting updates — by default, the last write wins. Service-managed failover can promote another region if the write region goes down.

Replication between regions is asynchronous, so physics forces a choice: how fresh must a read be, and how much latency and cost will you accept for it? Cosmos DB gives you five consistency levels, from strongest to weakest:

Level | What a reader is promised | Nusantara Retail use | Price of the promise
Strong | Always the latest committed write | Stock count for the very last batik in a flash sale | Reads cost about twice the RUs; across regions every write waits for all regions; not allowed with multi-region writes
Bounded staleness | Lags behind by at most K versions or T seconds | Live sale dashboard that may be up to a minute old | Reads cost about twice the RUs
Session (default) | Within one session you always read your own writes, in order | Dewi edits a price and sees her change immediately | Same cost as the weaker levels
Consistent prefix | Never sees writes out of order, but may lag | An order's status timeline | Single-replica reads
Eventual | No ordering guarantee; replicas converge over time | Product view counters and "likes" | Cheapest and fastest

The default level is set on the account, and you can change it at any time. A client can then ask for a weaker level for its own requests, but never a stronger one. Session is the default because it suits most applications: a user always sees their own changes, while reads stay as cheap and fast as eventual.

Consistency also shapes disaster recovery. If a whole region is lost, the writes that hadn't replicated yet are lost with it. Microsoft's documentation puts that window at under 15 minutes for session, consistent prefix and eventual in a multi-region account, and at zero for strong — which is exactly why strong consistency makes every write wait for the other regions. Multi-region accounts also raise the availability SLA, up to 99.999% depending on the configuration. Lunch 17 calls this window the recovery point objective.

Pause and think: During the 12.12 flash sale, the price of a batik shirt drops at exactly 00:00. Shoppers in Singapore are served from the Southeast Asia replica. Is a few seconds of old price acceptable, or must every shopper see the new price instantly? Which level would you choose — and what would it cost?

5. How it fits together for Nusantara Retail

Three more features make Cosmos DB pleasant to work with:

- Automatic indexing. By default every property of every item is indexed, so new fields like roastLevel are queryable the moment they appear — no index design required. To save RUs on write-heavy containers, you can exclude paths you never filter on.
- Change feed. Every container keeps an ordered record of inserts and updates (ordered per partition key). An Azure Function (Lunch 14) can react to it: refresh the search index, or tell waiting shoppers that a sold-out batik is back in stock. By default deletes don't appear; a mode that captures them requires continuous backup.
- Built-in backups. Every account is backed up automatically. The default periodic mode takes a full backup every four hours and keeps the latest two; continuous mode adds point-in-time restore for the last 7 or 30 days. Lunch 17 puts these into a disaster recovery plan.

So which database should Nusantara Retail use? Both, each for what it does best:

Choose Azure SQL when… | Choose Azure Cosmos DB when…
Data is naturally relational: orders, payments, invoices | Records vary in shape: catalogues, profiles, carts
You need joins, reports and transactions across many tables | You read and write by key at very high speed
One region (plus a DR copy) is enough | Users on several continents need local reads, or local writes
Your team already thinks in T-SQL | You want elastic throughput, from serverless to millions of RU/s

The design you will build in the lab: a Cosmos DB for NoSQL account with a catalog database and a products container partitioned by /category. Dewi's storefront reads a category page with one single-partition query and a product page with one point read. Development uses serverless, because it costs nearly nothing when idle; production would move to autoscale before the sale, with a ceiling sized from measured RUs. The app authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID and a Cosmos DB data-plane role (Lunch 05 and Lunch 15), not with account keys.

Production would live in Indonesia Central for data residency. Product names and prices aren't personal data, so a read region in Southeast Asia could serve shoppers abroad — carts holding customer IDs deserve a residency check first.

Before you build, learn from the mistakes teams make most often with their first Cosmos DB app:

- Running every page as a SELECT * across all partitions. It works on day one with 30 items and gets slower and more expensive with every product you add. Point reads and single-partition queries keep the cost flat.
- Pasting account keys into configuration files. A key opens every database in the account, and it never expires. Use Microsoft Entra ID with a data-plane role, and disable key-based authentication once nothing needs it.
- Creating databases and containers from application code. Treat them as infrastructure: create them with the CLI or Bicep (Lunch 20), and give the app a data role that can read and write items but not reshape the account.
- Forgetting TTL. Abandoned carts and expired sessions pile up and cost storage forever unless a TTL removes them.
- Leaving provisioned throughput on idle test containers. 400 RU/s bills every hour, used or not; serverless or the free tier is kinder to a development budget.

Field notes from Stefanus

Read the receipt on every request. Cosmos DB reports the price of every operation in its response, and I treat that number like a receipt. From the first sprint I ask teams to log the request charge next to the name of each query, and in design reviews I ask one question: which of your five busiest queries gets more expensive as the data grows? A point read costs the same with thirty items or thirty million, and a single-partition query grows only with its own partition. A cross-partition search grows with everything, and in a small test account with one physical partition it hides perfectly. So I test with data shaped like sale day, not like the demo, and I compare documents loaded with documents returned. When those two numbers drift apart, the bill is about to follow.

Go further

- Microsoft Learn: Partitioning and horizontal scaling in Azure Cosmos DB (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cosmos-db/partitioning) — logical and physical partitions, anti-patterns and the partition key strategies side by side.
- Microsoft Learn: Consistency levels in Azure Cosmos DB (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cosmos-db/consistency-levels) — the precise guarantees behind each level, including quorum reads and the RPO of each choice.
- Microsoft Learn: Request Units in Azure Cosmos DB (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/cosmos-db/request-units) — what drives RU charges and how capacity modes bill them.

quiz.q: Dewi adds a new product type almost every week, each with its own attributes. The team is starting a new service from scratch. Which Cosmos DB API should they choose?
quiz.a: API for NoSQL. It stores schema-free JSON items, indexes new properties automatically and gets new features first; the other APIs mainly exist to move existing MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin or Table apps across.

quiz.q: An orders container is partitioned by /storeId. During the 12.12 sale, writes for the online store fail with HTTP 429, even though the container's total RU/s are far from used up. What is happening, and what would you change?
quiz.a: A hot partition. One key value (the online store) receives most writes and hits the per-partition ceiling while other partitions idle. Re-create the container with a high-cardinality key such as /customerId (or hierarchical keys) and copy the data, because a partition key can't be changed in place.

quiz.q: Your lab subscription already has a free-tier Cosmos DB account from a past experiment. You want a short-lived account for a 45-minute lab that costs almost nothing. What do you choose?
quiz.a: A serverless account. Free tier is limited to one account per subscription and can't be added later, while serverless bills only the request units you actually consume plus storage.

quiz.q: Dewi must always see her own price changes immediately; other shoppers can lag a little. Which consistency level is the cheapest that meets the need?
quiz.a: Session, the default. It guarantees read-your-own-writes within a session while keeping single-replica reads, so reads don't cost the double RUs of strong or bounded staleness.

quiz.q: The finance team needs month-end reports joining payments, invoices and refunds, with transactions that update all three together. Cosmos DB or Azure SQL?
quiz.a: Azure SQL. The data is relational and needs multi-table joins and transactions; in Cosmos DB, transactions are limited to items that share one partition key value.

takeaways: Cosmos DB is a fully managed NoSQL database; choose API for NoSQL for new apps, because the API can't be changed after the account is created.
Everything costs request units: a 1 KB point read is 1 RU, and you pay for them through provisioned, autoscale or serverless capacity — plus one free-tier account per subscription.
The partition key is a one-way door: pick a property with many values that spreads traffic evenly and appears in your most common queries, or you'll build a hot partition.
Five consistency levels trade freshness against latency and cost; session is the default and the right answer for most apps.
Use Cosmos DB for flexible, fast, globally distributed data such as catalogues and carts, and keep relational, transaction-heavy data like orders and payments in Azure SQL.

lab.title: A product catalogue that scales
lab.text:
What you'll build

Nusantara Retail's web shop sells coffee, tea, batik, snacks, spices and crafts, and every category describes its products differently: coffee has a roast and a grind, batik has a technique, a fabric and a motif. You give the catalogue a home that doesn't force one table shape on all of them: a serverless Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL account with a database catalog and a container products partitioned by /category. You give yourself access to the data with Microsoft Entra ID instead of account keys, load 30 products with a small Python program that uses the azure-cosmos SDK, and then measure what things cost: a point read, a single-partition query and a cross-partition query, each with its request charge in RU. You change the default consistency level and watch the price of a read change, and finally you fix a search query that reads the whole catalogue to answer a question about coffee.

Before you start

- An Azure subscription where you can create resources (see Lab 01 (https://stefpin.github.io/azure-fundamentals-lunches/en/labs/01-before-you-begin.html)). Contributor on the subscription or resource group is enough: the data-plane role in Task 3 is a Cosmos DB setting, not an Azure role assignment.
- Azure Cloud Shell (Bash) — open shell.azure.com. It already has the Azure CLI and Python 3; Task 4 installs two Python packages into your home directory.
- Get the lab files and load the shared settings and this lab's names:

git clone https://github.com/stefpin/azure-fundamentals-lunches.git   # first time only
cd azure-fundamentals-lunches/labs/12-cosmos-db
source ../common/config.sh
source lab.env
echo "Account: $ACCOUNT  ·  endpoint: $COSMOS_ENDPOINT"

- If this subscription has never used Cosmos DB, register its resource provider (it takes a minute or two and is harmless to repeat):

az provider register --namespace Microsoft.DocumentDB --wait

Tip: Cloud Shell ends a session after about 20 minutes without activity, and variables disappear with it. If that happens, cd back into the lab folder and run the block above again (skip the git clone).

Important: A serverless account bills only for the request units you consume and the storage you use, so this lab costs next to nothing. Finish with the Clean up section anyway, even if you stop halfway.

Choose your mode

Mode | For you if… | How
Guided | you want every step explained | follow Tasks 1–6 below
Challenge | you already know the basics | read only the Challenge brief, build it your way, then run bash verify.sh

Task 1 · Create a serverless account for the API for NoSQL

The account is the top of the Cosmos DB hierarchy: it owns the endpoint, the regions, the consistency level and the billing model. You choose two things now that are hard or impossible to change later: the API (NoSQL) and the capacity mode. This lab uses serverless, and here is why:

| Serverless (this lab) | Provisioned throughput with the free tier
You pay for | the RUs your requests actually consume, plus storage | RU/s reserved every hour (the first 1,000 RU/s and 25 GB are free for the account's lifetime)
Available to | every subscription | one account per subscription, chosen at creation; your free tier may already be in use
Regions | one region only; you can't add regions later | as many as you like, each billed
Good for | development, tests, small or spiky traffic | steady traffic, several regions, production

Serverless works in any subscription and costs almost nothing for a lab that runs a few hundred requests. The trade-off is that it stays in one region; the Stretch goals show a second region on a separate, provisioned account.

az group create --name "$RG" --location "$LOCATION" \
  --tags course="$COURSE_TAG" lunch=12 --output table

az cosmosdb create \
  --name "$ACCOUNT" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --kind GlobalDocumentDB \
  --locations regionName="$LOCATION" failoverPriority=0 isZoneRedundant=False \
  --capabilities EnableServerless \
  --default-consistency-level Session \
  --output none

--kind GlobalDocumentDB is the API for NoSQL (it's also the default). Creating an account takes about 3–10 minutes: a good moment to reread Partitioning in the Lunch 12 reading.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Portal path: Home › Create a resource › Azure Cosmos DB › Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL › Create. Pick resource group rg-lunch12-<suffix>, account name cosmos-nusa-<suffix>, your region, and Capacity mode: Serverless. Leave the other tabs at their defaults — then come back and continue with Task 2.

Checkpoint: the account exists, speaks NoSQL, is serverless and uses Session consistency:

az cosmosdb show -g "$RG" -n "$ACCOUNT" --query "{api:kind, capabilities:capabilities[].name, \
  consistency:consistencyPolicy.defaultConsistencyLevel, regions:locations[].locationName, \
  endpoint:documentEndpoint}" --output jsonc

Expect "api": "GlobalDocumentDB", "capabilities": ["EnableServerless"], "consistency": "Session", one region, and an endpoint that matches $COSMOS_ENDPOINT.

Task 2 · Create the catalog database and the products container

A database groups containers; a container holds the items and is where you choose the partition key, the property Cosmos DB hashes to decide where every item lives. Nusantara Retail browses its catalogue by category (every shop page is one category) and each category holds at most a few thousand products, far below the 20 GB a logical partition can hold. So /category is a good fit for the catalogue. It would be a poor key for the order history, where one category would collect millions of writes during the 12.12 sale; that container would use something like /customerId instead.

az cosmosdb sql database create \
  --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --name "$DATABASE" --output none

az cosmosdb sql container create \
  --account-name "$ACCOUNT" --resource-group "$RG" \
  --database-name "$DATABASE" --name "$CONTAINER" \
  --partition-key-path "$PARTITION_KEY" --output none

There is no --throughput: serverless containers have none to set. And the partition key is permanent. To change it later you would copy every item into a new container.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Portal path: your Cosmos DB account › Data Explorer › New Container. Database id: Create new catalog; container id products; partition key /category — then come back and continue with Task 3.

Checkpoint: the container exists with the right partition key and default (consistent) indexing:

az cosmosdb sql container show -a "$ACCOUNT" -g "$RG" -d "$DATABASE" -n "$CONTAINER" \
  --query "{name:name, partitionKey:resource.partitionKey.paths[0], indexing:resource.indexingPolicy.indexingMode}" \
  --output jsonc

Expect "partitionKey": "/category" and "indexing": "consistent".

Task 3 · Give yourself data access with Microsoft Entra ID

Cosmos DB has two planes. The control plane (create accounts, containers, settings) uses ordinary Azure roles such as Contributor. The data plane (read and write items) uses Cosmos DB's own role system: being Owner of the subscription does not let you read a single product with your Entra identity. You need a data-plane role. There are two built-in ones; list them:

az cosmosdb sql role definition list -a "$ACCOUNT" -g "$RG" \
  --query "[].{role:roleName, id:name}" --output table

You'll see Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader and Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor. Give the contributor role to yourself, scoped to the whole account (/). You could also scope it to /dbs/catalog or to a single container:

ME=$(my_object_id)
az cosmosdb sql role assignment create \
  --account-name "$ACCOUNT" \
  --resource-group "$RG" \
  --scope "/" \
  --principal-id "$ME" \
  --role-definition-name "$DATA_ROLE" \
  --output none

Note: The portal's Access control (IAM) page manages control-plane Azure roles. It doesn't show this data-plane assignment, which is why this task uses the CLI.

Checkpoint: one assignment for your object ID:

az cosmosdb sql role assignment list -a "$ACCOUNT" -g "$RG" \
  --query "[?principalId=='$ME'].{role:roleDefinitionId, scope:scope}" --output table

The role column ends in /sqlRoleDefinitions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002, the built-in Data Contributor. New assignments can take a few minutes before requests succeed.

Fallback only: your organisation blocks the assignment? Use an account key, and know what you give up.

If role assignment create fails with an authorisation error and you can't get the permission, the scripts also accept the account's primary key:

export COSMOS_KEY=$(az cosmosdb keys list -g "$RG" -n "$ACCOUNT" --query primaryMasterKey --output tsv)

The trade-off: a primary key is a shared secret with full read and write access to every database in the account. It doesn't record who used it, it never expires on its own, and anyone who sees it in a screenshot or your shell history has the whole catalogue. Rotating it breaks every app that uses it. An Entra identity is per person (or per managed identity for apps), can be scoped to one container, and is removed in one command. That's why production accounts often switch keys off entirely (see the stretch goals). When you finish, run unset COSMOS_KEY.

Task 4 · Install the SDK and load the catalogue

The two scripts in app/ use the Azure Cosmos DB SDK for Python. azure-identity lets them reuse your Azure CLI sign-in, so there is no password or key in the code. Install both into your home directory:

pip install --user azure-cosmos azure-identity

app/products.json holds 30 products: five per category, each with the common fields (id, category, name, price in rupiah, stock) and an attributes object whose shape depends on the category. Load them:

python3 app/load_products.py

Writing 30 items to catalog/products (partition key /category)
Signed in with: Microsoft Entra ID (your Azure CLI / Cloud Shell sign-in)

  upsert p-coffee-001           [coffee]    x.xx RU
  ...
Done: 30 items written for ... RU (about ... RU per write).
Items per logical partition (category): batik=5, coffee=5, crafts=5, snacks=5, spices=5, tea=5

Each write is an upsert, so running the script again overwrites the same 30 items instead of duplicating them. Notice that a write costs several RU, more than a read: by default Cosmos DB indexes every property of every item, so each write also updates the index. That's also why you never declared a schema or an index for the batik motif or the coffee roast.

Tip: Prefer the portal? Open Data Explorer › catalog › products › Items to browse what you loaded. Open two items from different categories and compare their attributes.

Checkpoint: the container counts 30 items:

python3 app/query_products.py count

A message ending in HTTP 403 means the role from Task 3 hasn't taken effect yet: wait two minutes and run the loader again.

Task 5 · Point read, single-partition query, cross-partition query

A Cosmos DB bill is mostly a sum of request charges, so how you ask for data matters as much as how much data you have. Run the three ways of finding coffee side by side:

python3 app/query_products.py compare

Operation                                      Scope             Items      RU
---------------------------------------------- ----------------- ----- -------
Point read  id='p-coffee-001', key='coffee'    one item              1    1.00
Query  WHERE c.category = 'coffee'             single partition      5    x.xx
Query  WHERE c.price < 50000                   cross-partition      13    x.xx

The query charges depend on your data and SDK version (a few RU each). What they show:

- Point read (id and partition key): Cosmos DB goes straight to one item without running the query engine. An item up to 1 KB costs 1 RU. It's the cheapest way to fetch anything, which is why good designs know both values.
- Single-partition query: the partition key in the filter sends the query to one logical partition and its index.
- Cross-partition query: with no partition key, the query fans out to every physical partition. The script prints how many your container has: just 1 at this size, so the extra cost is small. A big catalogue spread over dozens of physical partitions pays a few RU, and some latency, for every partition the query visits.

Run each query on its own to see the details the script collects:

python3 app/query_products.py read p-coffee-001 coffee
python3 app/query_products.py query "SELECT c.id, c.name, c.price FROM c WHERE c.price < 50000"
python3 app/query_products.py query "SELECT c.id, c.name, c.price FROM c WHERE c.category = 'tea'" --pk tea

Each query also prints Documents the engine had to load next to documents returned. Remember that pair; it's the key to the Break-and-fix exercise.

Tip: Prefer the portal? In Data Explorer › products › New SQL Query, run SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.category = 'coffee' and open the Query Stats tab: it shows the request charge, the retrieved document count and the output document count.

Checkpoint: you can say, using your own numbers, why the point read is the cheapest, and what the script printed as the number of physical partitions.

Task 6 · Change the default consistency level

The account's default consistency is Session: you always read your own writes, and reads are served by a single replica. Strong and Bounded staleness read from two replicas to guarantee their promise, so the same read costs about twice as much. Switch the default to Strong, which takes a minute or two:

az cosmosdb update -g "$RG" -n "$ACCOUNT" --default-consistency-level Strong --output none
python3 app/query_products.py read p-coffee-001 coffee

The first line now says consistency: account default (Strong) and the point read costs about 2 RU. A client can also relax consistency for its own requests without touching the account:

python3 app/query_products.py read p-coffee-001 coffee --consistency Eventual

Back to about 1 RU. It only works in that direction: a client can choose the account default or anything weaker, never something stronger. Put the default back to Session, the right choice for a shop where every shopper must see their own basket:

az cosmosdb update -g "$RG" -n "$ACCOUNT" --default-consistency-level Session --output none

Tip: Prefer the portal? Portal path: your Cosmos DB account › Settings › Default consistency — pick a level and Save, then come back and run the same read commands.

Checkpoint: the account is back on Session:

az cosmosdb show -g "$RG" -n "$ACCOUNT" --query consistencyPolicy.defaultConsistencyLevel --output tsv

Break it and fix it

A developer builds the search box on the coffee page of the web shop. It works, so it ships:

python3 app/query_products.py query \
  "SELECT c.id, c.category, c.name, c.price FROM c WHERE CONTAINS(LOWER(c.name), 'kopi')"

Look at the last lines of the output. The scope is cross-partition, the engine loaded all 30 documents to return 6, and one of the 6 is a snack (Dodol Kopi) that doesn't belong on the coffee page. With 30 products the waste is a few RU. Now give the catalogue 10 synthetic copies of every product (330 items) and run the same query again:

python3 app/load_products.py --copies 10
python3 app/query_products.py query \
  "SELECT c.id, c.category, c.name, c.price FROM c WHERE CONTAINS(LOWER(c.name), 'kopi')"

The documents loaded and the RU grow with the whole catalogue, on every keystroke of every shopper. Your job: make the coffee search cheap, and make its cost grow only with the coffee category.

Hint

Two separate problems. The query doesn't tell Cosmos DB which logical partition to search. And wrapping the property in LOWER() stops the index from helping, so every document has to be loaded and lower-cased. CONTAINS has a third argument for case-insensitive matching.

Fix

python3 app/query_products.py query \
  "SELECT c.id, c.category, c.name, c.price FROM c WHERE c.category = 'coffee' AND CONTAINS(c.name, 'kopi', true)" \
  --pk coffee

The scope is now single partition, the documents loaded fall to the coffee products only, the request charge drops, and the snack is gone from the results. LOWER() and UPPER() can't use the index, so the engine must load every document. CONTAINS(..., true) does the case-insensitive match itself. If a search really must cover every category, store a lower-case copy of the name when you write the item and filter on that property instead. Microsoft's query-tuning guidance notes that the partition-key saving becomes large on big containers (around 100 GB or 30,000 RU/s and up); the habit is worth having long before that.

The copies are harmless and verify.sh doesn't mind them. Clean-up removes them with everything else.

Verify your work

bash verify.sh

Every check should say PASS. If one fails, the message tells you which task to revisit. The script only reads: it counts the items through the same Python code you used, so the SDK from Task 4 must be installed.

Clean up (do not skip!)

bash cleanup.sh

This deletes the resource group rg-lunch12-<suffix> and with it the account, its database, its items and the data-plane role assignment, which lives inside the account. Nothing was created outside the resource group. Deletion continues in the background for a few minutes. If you used the key fallback, also run unset COSMOS_KEY.

Troubleshooting

Symptom | Likely cause | Fix
az cosmosdb create fails with Sorry, we are currently experiencing high demand in Southeast Asia region… | Not enough capacity in that region right now | Repeat the command with another region, for example regionName=eastasia or regionName=indonesiacentral; the resource group can stay where it is
az cosmosdb create says the name is already in use | Account names are global DNS names | export LAB12_ACCOUNT=cosmos-nusa-<something-unique>, run source lab.env again and repeat Task 1
A script prints Cosmos DB refused the request (HTTP 403) with does not have required RBAC permissions to perform action [Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/readMetadata] | No data-plane role yet, or it hasn't taken effect | Check Task 3's checkpoint; if the assignment is there, wait a few minutes and retry
Could not get a Microsoft Entra token from the Azure CLI | The CLI isn't signed in (running on your own PC), or the Cloud Shell session expired | Run az login (PC) or restart Cloud Shell, then source the two files again
The Azure Cosmos DB SDK for Python is not installed | Task 4's pip install didn't run in this environment | pip install --user azure-cosmos azure-identity
pip stops with error: externally-managed-environment (some Linux and macOS installs) | Your Python is managed by the operating system | Use a virtual environment: python3 -m venv ~/.venv-lab12 && source ~/.venv-lab12/bin/activate && pip install azure-cosmos azure-identity
Set COSMOS_ENDPOINT first | New shell: the variables are gone | cd into the lab folder and run source ../common/config.sh and source lab.env again
Not found (HTTP 404) from read | Wrong id or wrong partition key, for example read p-coffee-001 tea | A point read needs both, spelled exactly; values are case-sensitive
Free-tier stretch goal fails because the subscription already has a free-tier account | Only one free-tier account per subscription | Find it with az cosmosdb list --query "[?enableFreeTier].{name:name, rg:resourceGroup}" --output table, or skip the stretch goal (without the free tier it costs money every hour)

Build the following, any way you like (portal, CLI, Bicep):

1. A Cosmos DB for NoSQL account in rg-lunch12-<suffix> (name it cosmos-nusa-<suffix>) that is serverless, or provisioned with the free tier, and uses Session as its default consistency.
